Le, les e os outros pronomes de objeto i: Le, les, and the other indirect object pronouns
PASSO 1: o objeto indireto responde à pe: STEP 1: the indirect object answers the question «to whom?» or «for whom?» after the verb. In «Doy un libro a Ana», I give the book to whom? To Ana. The book is the direct object; Ana is the indirect object. STEP 2: the indirect object pronouns are «me» (me), «te» (you, tú), «le» (him, her, usted), «nos» (us), «os» (you-all, vosotros), and «les» (them, ustedes). Only the third person differs from the direct object of lesson 23: here it's «le, les», and there it was «lo, la, los, las». STEP 3: «le» and «les» don't change for gender: «Le doy un libro» works for «a ella» and for «a él». STEP 4: the position is the same as the direct object: before the conjugated verb («Le escribo») or attached to the infinitive («Quiero escribirle»). STEP 5: the pronoun shows up even when the person's name is also in the sentence: «Le doy el libro a Ana», «Les escribo a mis padres». That isn't redundancy — it's simply the normal way to speak. STEP 6: for emphasis or contrast, add «a mí», «a ti», «a él», «a ella», «a usted», «a nosotros», «a vosotros», «a ellos», «a ustedes»: «A mí me dio un libro y a ti no». STEP 7: an English speaker tends to translate "to her" literally and reach for just «a ella», leaving out the pronoun: «Dije a ella». The correct form always keeps the pronoun too: «le dije». STEP 8: the same pronouns show up with «gustar», which you've already seen: «A Ana le gusta el té» and «Me gusta el té».
o português do Brasil costuma dizer «dei: English marks the indirect object with word order instead of a required pronoun: «I gave her the book» or «I gave the book to her» both work, and the sentence is complete without any extra marker once "her" appears. Spanish never drops that marker: «le di el libro» keeps «le» in place even though «a ella» may also be stated outright, so the habit of skipping the pronoun once the person is already named — which feels natural in English — has to be unlearned for Spanish.

Direto ou indireto, e falsos amigos: Direct or indirect, and false friends
PASSO 1: para decidir entre os dois pron: STEP 1: to decide between the two pronouns, ask the verb. "What? Whom?" points to the direct object («lo, la»). "To whom? For whom?" points to the indirect object («le, les»). «Escribí una carta» answers what was written; «Le escribí una carta» also answers to whom. STEP 2: verbs that almost always take an indirect object: dar, decir, escribir, contar, preguntar, responder, pedir, prestar, enseñar, ofrecer, regalar, explicar, mostrar, mandar, enviar, and also «gustar, interesar, encantar, doler, parecer». «Me duele la cabeza» (my head hurts — literally, the head hurts to me). STEP 3: verbs that take a direct object when it's a person: llamar, ayudar, esperar, visitar, invitar, escuchar, ver, conocer. «La llamo», «Lo ayudo». STEP 4: «preguntar» and «responder» take the indirect object, unlike how English sometimes treats them: «Le pregunté su nombre» and «Le respondí ayer» — English "I asked her" and "I answered him" look like direct objects, but Spanish treats the person as indirect here. STEP 5: «pedir» also takes the indirect object for the person being asked: «Le pedí un café al camarero». «Pedir prestado» means to borrow; «prestar» means to lend, not to render a service: «Le pedí prestado el coche» and «Le presté el coche». STEP 6: false friends: «apellido» is last name/surname, not nickname, which is «apodo» or «mote»: «Mi apellido es Rosa; mi apodo es Rosi». «Regalar» means to give as a gift, and «un regalo» is a gift — not a perk or a pleasure. «Pegar» means to hit or to glue, not to catch: «Le pegó a su hermano» means "he hit his brother". «Enseñar» means to teach and also to show: «Me enseñó su casa» means "he showed me his house". STEP 7: in Latin America, word order and the pronouns stay the same; what changes is «os», which doesn't exist there. Instead of «os escribo», you say «les escribo».
o português também separa o direto do in: English also keeps direct and indirect objects distinct in form sometimes («I saw her» versus «I gave her the book»), but everyday speech blurs the line by letting a single pronoun like "her" do double duty in both roles. Spanish keeps the split sharp no matter the context: «la vi» (direct) and «le di» (indirect) never swap. The false friends in this part can trip up an English speaker in a very specific way: «apellido» isn't close to a nickname, «prestar» has nothing to do with being "prestigious", and «pegar» has nothing to do with "pegging" something — it means to hit or stick.

Pedir e oferecer com «me», e esclarecer: Asking and offering with «me», and clarifying «le»
PASSO 1: para pedir algo educadamente, u: STEP 1: to ask for something politely, use «me» with an action verb: «¿Me trae la cuenta?», «¿Me pone un café?», «¿Me puede ayudar?». The «me» marks that the request is for you. STEP 2: to offer, use «te» or «le»: «¿Te ayudo?», «¿Le ayudo, señora?», «¿Le pongo algo más?». STEP 3: with «usted», «le» doesn't say the gender. If you need to, clarify: «Le dije a usted, no a ella». STEP 4: to clarify an ambiguous «le», add «a + person»: «Le escribí a Marta», «Les mandamos una invitación a sus padres». STEP 5: with the verb «contestar», the indirect object is the person: «Le contesté a Ana» (I answered Ana). To answer the phone, you say «contestar el teléfono». STEP 6: in the indefinido, the forms are the usual ones, with the pronoun in front: «Le di», «Le dije», «Le escribí», «Nos mandaron».
em português, «me traz a conta?», «te aj: English politeness formulas like "could you bring me the check?" and "can I help you?" put the pronoun in roughly the same spot Spanish does, so the basic shape transfers fine. What doesn't transfer is that Spanish courtesy phrasing is more direct about who's asking: «¿Le ayudo?» to a customer, «¿Me trae la cuenta?» to a waiter — there's no softening "would you mind" built into the grammar the way English speakers often add one.
